summary.en: The creator turned a 2D cartoon-style concept into a vertical ad creative. The prompt specifies drawing every frame in an HTML canvas and using code, voice tools, FFmpeg, and browser rendering.

prompt.text:
<inputs>
Ask me for: the product (a real one I give you, or invent a fake brand so there are no brand issues), the genre the story hides inside (detective, alien invasion, heist, nature doc, cooking show), and where it will be posted (it decides the follow handle). If I have no idea, pitch me 3 "What if" stories that each hide the product inside a genre, and let me pick. Ask which voice tool I have: ElevenLabs (about 1,000 credits a Short) or free Kokoro run locally. Tell me no image or video model is needed, because every frame is drawn in code. Then show me the script with word counts and seconds per line, a rough storyboard, and a cast sheet before anything costs money.
</inputs>

<direction>
A 1080x1920, 60 fps, 40-45 s vertical Short: a 2D "What if" kid cartoon that is secretly an ad, drawn entirely on an HTML canvas in code. Not 3D, not AI images, not a Roblox look. It borrows the big What-if channels' rhythm (DAY/CASE cards, a HUD counter, poofs, pop-in captions, a rewind loop) but every character and outfit is original.
The ad formula (from the best Pixar-style AI ads):
- Cold open in a genre with no product mention for the first beats; the viewer thinks it is a story.
- The product enters as a plot device (the evidence, the stolen thing, the reason someone wins), never as an ad.
- The twist is the product's benefit turned into a punchline ("too good to share", "too hard to kill").
- End on one glossy packshot: the product spinning in on a sunburst with a 2-line tagline.
Characters: short, chibi, cartoony, one shared rig for the whole cast.
- Big round head (radius 150 at scale 1, slightly wider than tall), small pear-shaped body, stubby rounded legs and arms ending in round mitten hands, oval shoes with a coloured sole. Adults are taller (1.2-1.3x body), little siblings 0.82x.
- Every shape has an 8 px #2a1b3d outline and one soft darker shade on its right edge only (a thin crescent, never half the face).
- Hair is smooth rounded shapes: a cap that covers the whole crown, a soft side swoop, a bowl cut, a side part, a ponytail hanging BEHIND the head. Never spikes or zigzags.
- Give every character their own outfit; never copy a reference creator's character clothes 1:1. Example cast: detective kid (tan belted trench coat, red scarf wrap, brown fedora with a band), little brother (red-white striped tee, blue overalls, bowl cut), Mom (black hair, yellow headband, ponytail, coral sweater, green pants), Dad (side part, short jaw beard, round thin glasses, green sweater vest, white shirt, blue tie), dog (white with a brown eye patch and floppy brown ears).
- Faces carry the comedy. Eyes: normal (white with a big pupil and two highlights), huge, happy arcs, closed, star, spiral, narrow. Brows: up, worry, angry, flat (mirror them per eye so worry never reads as angry). Mouths: smile, grin, wide, scream (one clean open shape with teeth band and tongue), o, flat, smirk, wavy, chew (puffed cheeks). Plus blush, sweat drops and sunglasses that drop in. Blink for 0.1 s about every 1.6 s. Mouths flap only while that character's words are being spoken.
Sets: detailed flat rooms in saturated colours with thick outlines, each with a night version (darker blue grade plus warm lamp glows): a kitchen (wallpaper, upper cabinets, window with curtains and sky, jar shelf, plant, clock, pendant lamp, tiled backsplash, drawer counter, checker floor) and a bedroom (striped wall, window, poster, toy shelf, bed with a star blanket, nightstand lamp, plank floor, rug). Bursting sunburst colours for montages and the packshot.
Fonts (all free, from Google Fonts' GitHub repo):
- Captions: Lilita One.
- Day/CASE cards and big world words: Luckiest Guy.
- The product wrapper text: Sniglet ExtraBold, auto-fitted so it never clips.
Captions:
- 1-2 words at a time in Lilita One 94 px, centred at y 1600 (on the legs, never across a face), max 900 px wide.
- White with a 20 px #1c1030 outline and a soft shadow, popping from 55% to 100% in 0.16 s.
- Key words in caps and colour: red #ff5165, green #5dff8f, yellow #ffd23f, pink #ff7ad9, cyan #7debff, orange #ffa53d, purple #c49bff.
- No full stops or commas on screen, ever. Hide captions on the packshot.
Fake game UI over the world:
- A HUD counter pill (260x92, centred at x 540, y 196) with a tiny product icon that tracks the story (snacks stolen, clues found) and ticks with a green "+N".
- CASE/DAY cards: Luckiest Guy 230 px in yellow #ffd23f with a 38 px outline, tilted -6 degrees, popping in over 0.22 s and leaving at 1.05 s.
- Toast pills (88 px tall at y 374), a FOLLOW button with the handle chip and a cursor that presses it (it turns green "FOLLOWING").
Motion: something moves on every line, and the picture changes every 1-3 s.
- Things arrive with a squash (0.72, 1.12, 0.95, 1 over 0.3 s), an overshoot ease or a white poof cloud with stars, never a plain fade.
- Characters breathe (1.2% squash) all the time.
- The camera pushes in 5-15% per shot, stays inside the set, and shakes (decaying over 0.35 s) on every hit.
Banned: real logos or real creators' characters, AI stills, spiky hair, a frame that holds still for more than 1 s, captions over faces, system fallback fonts, whispered narration.
</direction>

<structure>
Length: 40-45 s, 85-100 words, 14 lines. Times below are from the 40.3 s "Snack Detective" ad; key every beat to a real word.
0-5 s: the narrator reads the title as line 1 ("What if you were a detective and someone kept stealing your snacks?") over the striking picture (crime-scene tape round an empty drawer; the hero poofs in on "detective"; the drawer slides open empty).
5-8 s: the hero's line that proves it ("My Krunchkin bar! GONE!"): spiral eyes, scream, a toast pill ("CASE OPENED"), the HUD appears with +1.
8-13 s: CASE 1. Suspect one (little brother with chocolate on his face, a magnifier finds it) and a tiny excuse line ("It's paint!").
13-17 s: CASE 2, bigger. HUD +1. A second suspect (the dog) looks guilty, the wrapper slides out.
17-21 s: CASE 3, the biggest. HUD +3. A third suspect (Dad "on a diet", a bar in his pocket) with a callback pop-in of suspect one pointing.
21-24.5 s: the follow beat told inside the story ("Follow, and the detective gets one more clue"): the button is pressed about 0.5 s into the line and a clue card drops in.
24.5-26.5 s: the turn begins ("So you set a trap"): night, a spotlight on the product as bait.
26.5-29 s: a 3-shot montage with no voice (0.85 s each on bursting colours): DUST!, NIGHT CAM (green tint, REC), RING RING! The counter races to 999.
29-30 s: the hero's line ("Got you!"): flashlight snaps on. The music cuts dead.
30-35 s: the twist: the fridge light floods on, it is Mom, chewing ("They're too crunchy to share, sweetie"), sunglasses drop in.
35-37.5 s: the packshot ("Krunchkin. Too good to share."): the bar spins in, crumbs fly, TOO GOOD / TO SHARE pops in.
37.5-39.8 s: a short tag from the hero ("Wait, there's a whole box?") as Mom slides a giant box into frame, HUD +94.
last 0.55 s: REWIND. The whole film scrubs backwards to frame 0 with scanlines and a REWIND label, so the end loops into the start.
</structure>

<build>
1. Tools (free): Python 3 with numpy, scipy and Pillow, FFmpeg, Node with Playwright and its Chromium, faster-whisper large-v3-turbo (int8 on the CPU), git for fonts. Install what's missing and tell me what you installed.
2. Script and storyboard first:
- "you" and "your" point of view, the title as line 1, one picture per line, 10-16 words at most per line, words a 10-year-old uses, no names.
- Draw the storyboard with the real rig and real fonts (15 panels at 1080x1920, tiled with times, speaker and line), and a cast lineup. Zoom in on every character at full size and fix hair, hats, glasses, mouths and outfits before showing me.
3. Voice: ElevenLabs eleven_v3 with stock library voices, one take per character, all of that character's lines in one request separated by blank lines.
- Narrator: an energetic young male creator voice (Liam). Hero kid: a playful bright voice (Jessica). Mom: sassy (Laura). Little brother: the kid voice pitched up 3 semitones afterwards.
- Audio tags: [excited], [screaming], [nervously], [sweetly], [mischievously], [confused]. Write numbers as words ("Case one").
- Ask before spending credits. Check the API key's own credit cap before the big narrator request.
- Run faster-whisper with word timestamps on each take. Match lines by word count with difflib, refine each line's edges on the audio itself (pad 0.06 s before, 0.15 s after).
- Squeeze pauses inside a line to 0.22 s. Leave 0.2 s between lines, 0.33 s before each CASE line, and a 2.55 s silent slot for the montage.
- Level every take to the narrator's median. Word times on the finished track come from the take times plus the assembly offsets, so every cut, card, caption and sound starts on a real word.
4. Film (free): one HTML page with one canvas, where every frame is a pure function of time: https://window.seek/(t), window.READY, window.END.
- A SHOTS list of [start, end, function] keyed to word times (cuts land 0.04 s before their word). Each shot sets a camera (centre, zoom over time, clamped to the set), draws its world and characters, and the overlays (HUD, cards, toasts, follow button, captions) draw in screen space on top.
- One rig function draws every character from a pose: x, y, scale, squash, rotation, flip, arm and leg angles, head tilt, eyes, brows, mouth, look, blush, sweat, shades, prop. Hand positions come from the same arm maths, so props (magnifier, flashlight, product, salad, paintbrush) sit in the hand.
5. Check before render: contact sheets at the start and end of every line on the real timing. Fix captions over faces, props out of frame, cards over heads, camera past the set edge, and any text that clips.
6. Render (free): seek 120 subframes a second in headless Chromium, pipe JPEG screenshots to FFmpeg, blend pairs with tmix for motion blur at 60 fps (about 8 min for 40 s on 2 CPUs). Encode the upload copy with libx264 CRF 20, preset slow, AAC 256k (about 26 MB).
7. Sound (free, Mixkit):
- Music: one playful bed ("Comical"), about 19 dB under the voice. Cut it dead on the two big moments (the trap springing and the twist reveal), back on the packshot.
- Effects placed so each one's loudest moment lands on its frame: a poof on arrivals, pops and whooshes on cards, a coin ding on every counter tick, a glint on the magnifier, a boing on silly pop-ins, a slam on screams, a click and slam on the flashlight, a gasp and sting on the reveal, a crunch on the product, a party horn on the tagline, a rewind sound on the loop.
- Effects on speech 12 dB under the voice, in gaps 4 dB under. Measure voice versus everything else per line and duck the rest under any line below 15.5 dB (the worst line should end at 15.5 dB or more).
- Two-pass loudnorm to -14 LUFS, true peak -1.5.
8. Final checks: no frame still for over 1 s outside a deliberate beat, captions on their words, and a look at 15 frames across the finished file before delivering.
</build>

<gotchas>
- My workspace's own internet is blocked; fonts come from Google Fonts' GitHub repo with a sparse git clone (ofl/lilitaone, apache/luckiestguy, ofl/sniglet). Never fall back to DejaVu or another system font.
- A browser tab can call ElevenLabs but cannot save files into my folders. Record the voices with a small .bat on my PC that curls the API into the project's Raw folder, and runs faster-whisper there in the same double-click.
- An ElevenLabs API key can have its own credit cap below the account balance. A refused request returns quota_exceeded; log the response body so the reason is visible.
- Whisper writes "1" for "one" and drops "!" and "..."; match lines by word count, not exact text.
- Spiky or zig-zag hair always looks broken. Use smooth bezier hair caps whose top reaches above the head's crown, or the crown shows as a bald band.
- A ponytail drawn in front of the body covers held props; hang it behind the head on the far side.
- Square glasses crash into the brows; use round thin rims centred on the eyes with the brows above them.
- A hanging scarf tail reads as a tie; use a neck wrap with a small side knot.
- Big shading ellipses split faces in half; keep the shade a thin crescent on one edge.
- Plain script tags share one global scope: a page variable named like a helper function (window.N vs function N) blanks the whole page. Prefix names.
- A zoomed camera centre near the floor shows black past the set edge. Clamp the camera centre to the set for its zoom.
- Captions at y 1290 and 124 px covered faces in every close-up; 94 px at y 1600 sits on the legs.
- Hits placed on screamed words ("GONE!", "box?") pushed the voice under 15 dB; check per line and duck before normalising.
- The follow beat is one swappable shot: change the handle per platform and re-render only that.
</gotchas>

<start>
Ask me for the product and the genre, or pitch 3. Then show me the script (word count and seconds per line), the storyboard and the cast sheet before any voice is generated.
</start>

title.zh: 产品官网动态便当格功能展示

summary.zh: 为产品官网制作的动态 bento 功能网格，每个卡片用一段小动画演示对应功能。作者用 Opus 5.5 生成，并在帖子中公开了完整提示词。
summary.en: Animated bento feature grid for a product website, where each tile plays a small scene showing what the feature does. Generated with Opus 5.5 from a detailed prompt the creator shares in the post.

prompt.text:
# Small animations for a product site's feature tiles

Give every tile in my site's feature grid a small animation: a tiny scene that shows what the feature does.

## 0. Before you build
- Read the project: find out the tech stack (plain HTML/CSS, React, Vue, Svelte, Astro, Tailwind, Framer Motion…) and build it the way the project already does. Don't add an animation library unless the project already uses one.
- Ask me which look to use:
A. The Lumno material below, as written.
B. My product's own style: take the colors, radii, borders and shadows from my existing design tokens and components, and keep only the structure and motion rules from this prompt.
C. A mix: the Lumno material in my brand's accent color and radii.
- Picking features: if I named features, animate those. If not, read the product's site, docs or code, list 3–5 features that a short scene can explain, and let me pick.

## 1. Lumno material (option A)
Overall: quiet, neutral, precise. Hairlines instead of borders, soft shadows tinted warm, no gradients or color washes, one accent color.

- Grid: one card with an outer radius of 28px. Cells are separated by 1px hairlines (a 1px grid gap over a hairline color). Cells are white. The card has a faint hairline ring and a soft shadow.
- Art panel: inset 8px from the cell edge, with a radius of the card radius minus the inset (20px), so corners stay concentric.
- Fill #fafafa, plus an inner 1px ring: box-shadow: inset 0 0 0 1px rgba(32,38,46,.07).
- Texture: background: repeating-linear-gradient(-45deg, rgba(32,38,46,.06) 0 1px, transparent 1px 7px).
- The scene sits centred on the panel, about 126×118px.
- Text bars: body bars 4px tall with a 2px radius in #e5e9ef; heading bars 5px tall in #cdd4de. Vary the widths (34–92px).
- Mini windows and cards: white with a 9px radius.
- Shadow: 0 0 0 1px rgba(47,42,34,.06), 0 8px 20px -10px rgba(47,42,34,.25).
- Tab strip: 20px tall, #eef1f5. Tabs: 16px tall with 6px top corners; the active tab is white.
- Favicons: 10px.
- Inner surfaces such as charts or fields: #f4f6fa. Secondary data: #b9c9e0. Accent: #3462ad, used only on the result.
- Icon chip (top-left of each tile): 32px, 10px radius, 1px border rgba(32,38,46,.1), white, shadow 0 1px 2px rgba(32,38,46,.05), a line-style glyph in #4b5563.
- Text color: a warm near-black, #2f2a22.
- Hover: the cell darkens to about 2.5% grey; the panel goes to #f4f5f6 with its ring at .09; the icon chip grows 32→36px from its top-left corner, its glyph turns to the text color, and its shadow deepens slightly.
- Dark mode (suggested values; keep the same relationships):
- Cells #17181a, panel #1d1f22, inner ring rgba(255,255,255,.06), texture rgba(255,255,255,.04).
- Body bars #2c2f34, heading bars #3a3e45.
- Windows #24272b with a 1px rgba(255,255,255,.06) outline and a shadow of 0 8px 20px -10px rgba(0,0,0,.6).
- Tab strip #1a1c1f, accent #6f9bea, text #ecebe8.

## 2. Scene
- One idea per tile: 2–4 moves that show "action → result", such as "click → a small window opens" or "change here → the other side syncs".
- Abstract wireframes only: no screenshots and no real text. Use at most one small icon where something needs to be recognisable.
- Motion: ease-out for movement, cubic-bezier(.22,1,.36,1); a slight spring for appearing, cubic-bezier(.34,1.4,.64,1). Each move takes 250–600ms; the whole scene is done in about 3s.
- Icon chip: when the tile plays, its glyph redraws stroke by stroke (draw, pop or slide per part), then hands back to the solid icon.

## 3. Playback
- Resting styles are the final frame. Animations only describe where things come from (fill-mode: both or equivalent), so reduced motion shows the result and an interrupted play never jumps.
- The art panel fades in (opacity, plus translateY 6px and scale .97 to none) as its tile first plays.
- Play once in view: when about 70% of the tile is visible, wait ~200ms, then play. Tiles that enter together go ~250ms apart, in reading order. Stop on the final frame.
- One "played" state (a class or data attribute) drives every animation in the tile. To replay: remove it, force a reflow, add it back (or re-key in a framework).
- On mouse hover (mouse only) or keyboard focus, replay: blur the final frame out over ~160ms (blur 6px, opacity 0), restart under the blur, then clear it. Don't restart a play that hasn't finished.
- Optional loop on hover: while the pointer stays on the tile, replay again ~600ms after each play ends. When the pointer leaves, finish the current play and rest on the final frame.
- Touch: a tap follows the tile's link; nothing depends on hover.
- prefers-reduced-motion: reduce: no animation; show the final frame.

## 4. Colors and dark mode
- Every color is a variable on the art panel (panel, ring, texture, bars, windows, tab strip, accent, shadow); no hard-coded colors in the rules.
- Follow prefers-color-scheme, and the project's manual theme switch too (a class or data-theme), if it has one.
- Check it in both light and dark.

## 5. Delivery
- Mark the art as decorative (aria-hidden) and keep translatable text out of it.
- Check it in a real browser: first play, hover replay, keyboard focus, reduced motion, dark mode and a phone-width layout.

summary.zh: 这段 Claude Code 提示词规定了用 Blender 制作写实三维解说短片的完整流程，包括字幕、声音、渲染和检查。
summary.en: A long Claude Code prompt specifies a Blender pipeline for realistic 3D narrated Shorts with captions, sound, rendering, and validation.

prompt.text:
Ask me 2 things, then wait:
1. The story in one line: a strange TRUE event where one person did one odd physical thing ("He tied 42 weather balloons to a lawn chair."). If I say "you pick", pitch 3 with one source link each and take the first unless I choose.
2. The voice. Default: Kokoro (free, runs on my computer), a calm, warm male narrator.
Then tell me everything else is free: Blender (find my install, or tell me the one download), its free MPFB extension for human bodies (ask me before you install it) and into this folder a Python venv with FFmpeg (imageio-ffmpeg), kokoro-onnx + its model files (kokoro-v1.0.onnx and voices-v1.0.bin from the kokoro-onnx GitHub releases), faster-whisper (small.en), numpy and Pillow. It needs no API key or account and renders on my graphics card with EEVEE.
</inputs>

<direction>
The look: a clean, realistic 3D world, like a good game cutscene. Bright, saturated, a little filmic.
- People: realistic bodies with generic faces and big readable expressions (shock, a smirk, a scream). Plain clothes, no logos. Never a real person's likeness: for a real person keep the face out of close-ups (hands, back, side, distance, straight top-down).
- CALM shots only. Bodies in fast action or contact (running, jumping, fighting, falling) look stiff, so tell the story with frozen moments under a slowly moving camera, macro inserts of hands and objects, rooms, vehicles, the sky, top-down views and the aftermath.
- One new picture for every caption chunk (2-4 words, about 1-1.5 s): a new framing, a new action or a camera move. Nothing ever holds still: every shot drifts, pushes in or orbits.
- The shot kit: macro insert (extreme close-up of the key object or hands, very shallow depth of field), hero low angle (wide lens at waist height), god's-eye top-down with a slow rotate, tracked object, over the shoulder, smash zoom on the word that matters, whip pan between beats, glow highlight (the named object glows orange with a rim, then fades), a big 3D number lying in the scene, a thought bubble (a cloud ring showing what he hoped for), a TV in the scene replaying the event.
- Light: a bright warm sun, blue sky with clouds, soft shadows. Night scenes use hard lamps and a dark sky. Wide lens up close, depth of field on every shot, motion blur on every fast camera move.
- Captions: 2-4 words at a time, white bold rounded sans, about 64 px on a 1080 px-wide frame, centred, 78% down the frame, soft dark shadow, no box. Each chunk replaces the last on the same frame as its picture.
- Banned: real footage, photos, downloaded textures or 3D models, logos, AI images or AI video, downloaded music, gore.
</direction>

<structure>
38-50 s, 100-140 words, 150-180 words a minute. The voice starts at 0.0 s.
- Line 1: the most surprising physical act, in past tense, opening with "He" (or "She"). No name, date or setup. Frame 1 shows that act.
- Then a cause-and-effect chain: every sentence starts with a hinge word (Then, Suddenly, So, Because, But, Later) and is ONE visible action.
- The context arrives late, after "You see,".
- A reveal: someone looks closer and the story turns.
- The last line is the consequence. No call to action, no question.
- Names are rare: use one only when it pays off.
Title = "He ..." or "The Man Who ...". The cover is the first frame.
</structure>

<build>
Save every stage to disk so a crash never costs more than one stage.
- sources.md: every fact with its link and the date you read it. Anything you can't verify stays out.
- script.json: the lines and the caption chunks cut by hand (2-4 words, one picture each), each chunk with its shot: the set, the camera, what moves.
- https://voice.py/: Kokoro reads the whole script in one take (speed 1.0-1.1) and pauses are squeezed to 0.35 s at most; faster-whisper times every word (pass it a 16 kHz numpy array, not a path); write chunks.json with each chunk's start and end. A picture and its caption switch together on frame round(start*30)+1.
- blender/: Python scripts run headless (blender -b -P). https://build.py/ makes one .blend with the sets, the cast, the props and every shot baked with a key on every frame. https://look.py/ sets EEVEE with ray tracing, the AgX view with the Punchy look, motion blur, depth of field and bloom in the compositor. Bodies come from MPFB or are built by you; clothes, hair, props and sets are built in code.
- Stills first: one half-size still per shot as a contact sheet. Look at every tile and fix what's off before any full render. Time one full-size frame and tell me the estimate.
- Render 1080x1920 at 30 fps to PNG frames, skipping frames already on disk.
- https://sound.py/, numpy only: a light music bed, a sound on every action (a whoosh on each whip pan, hits, wind, room tone), ducked under the voice, mastered to -14 LUFS on the whole stereo mix.
- https://compose.py/: burn the captions in from chunks.json. Encode out/<slug>_9x16.mp4 (1080x1920, 30 fps, TV-range yuv420p) and out/<slug>_x_7x8.mp4 (1008x1152, under 10 MB, 2-pass): a crop of the 9:16 frame that keeps the subject and the caption.
</build>

<gotchas>
- Blender paths: pass absolute output paths (a relative one lands on the drive root).
- MPFB headless: enable it with addon_utils.enable("bl_ext.user_default.mpfb"). Bake a body's shape keys before you pose it: the rig is fitted to the baked shape.
- Clothes: cut them from the body mesh and push them 7-16 mm out along the normals; keep two rings of body faces under every hem.
- Nothing coplanar: keep every resting object 1 cm off its neighbour and draw ground markings into the texture, or they flicker.
- Hair: EEVEE draws hair only from a Curves object, hair type STRIP. Use a Principled BSDF on it (the Hair BSDF renders black).
- Skin: keep subsurface weight near 0.2 (more turns faces black in EEVEE) and add a soft fill light from below under a noon sun.
- Hands: a curled hand reads as a claw from the palm side, so shoot a grip from behind the knuckles.
- Motion blur: shutter position START, a key on every frame, plus a key half a frame after each shot's last frame, so blur never reaches across a cut.
- Check: run a black-frame and one-frame-flicker check on the render. Make a contact sheet (a frame every 0.5 s) and look at every tile: the act reads in the first 2 s, faces are lit, nothing clips through anything, captions stay off faces and key objects. Then step through the first 2 s, the middle and the end frame by frame. Fix, render only the changed shots again.
</gotchas>

<start>
Pitch (or take my story), then show me the script with the word count, the caption chunks with their seconds and the shot list with what the first frame shows. Build nothing until I say go.

summary.zh: 作者称这是用 Opus 5.5 和一个提示词制作的液态玻璃 3D 首页区块，包含可旋转立方体和折射标题，没有使用 Spline 或 Blender。
summary.en: A liquid-glass 3D hero section with a rotatable cuboid and refracted headline was made with Opus 5.5 from one prompt, without Spline, Blender, or a 3D designer.

prompt.text: Build a single standalone index.html file (inline CSS + inline JS, no local assets, no build step) containing ONE full-screen hero section: a black "Design World" landing hero with a rotatable 3D glass cuboid in the centre that refracts a huge background headline with chromatic dispersion. Recreate it exactly to the spec below. ================================================== 1. EXTERNAL RESOURCES (use these exact URLs) ================================================== - Font: Google Fonts Poppins, weights 300/400/500/600/700/800 - Three.js r169 via importmap: "three": "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/three@0.169.0/build/three.module.js" "three/addons/": "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/three@0.169.0/examples/jsm/" Imports: GLTFLoader (loaders/GLTFLoader.js), mergeVertices + mergeGeometries (utils/BufferGeometryUtils.js), RoundedBoxGeometry (geometries/RoundedBoxGeometry.js). - 3D model (rounded cube GLB, CORS-enabled, load directly, do NOT download or replace): const MODEL_URL = 'https://d8j0ntlcm91z4.cloudfront.net/user_38xzZboKViGWJOttwIXH07lWA1P/hf_20260929_212926_92423081-b0e4-4f5a-b650-14af6c05c058.glb'; If it fails to load, fall back to new RoundedBoxGeometry(1, 1, 1, 8, 0.12). Page : "Design World — Explore New Ideas". ================================================== 2. PAGE STRUCTURE (HTML) ================================================== <section class="hero" id="hero"> <canvas id="scene" aria-label="Rotatable glass cube. Drag to rotate."></canvas> <div class="ui"> <h1 class="sr-only">Explore New Ideas</h1> <header class="nav"> <a href="#" class="logo"><i class="logo-mark"></i><b>Design</b><span>World</span></a> <ul class="nav-links"><li><a>Home</a></li><li><a>Portfolio</a></li><li><a>Contact Us</a></li></ul> </header> <div class="arrows"> <button class="arrow" id="prev">[left-arrow SVG]</button> <button class="arrow" id="next">[right-arrow SVG]</button> </div> <nav class="dots"><button class="dot"></button><button class="dot active"></button><button class="dot"></button></nav> <p class="tagline">Let's Build the<br>Future of <strong>Design.</strong></p> <div class="cta-row"> <a href="#" class="cta">Explore Now</a> <span class="cta-line"></span> <span class="count" aria-hidden="true">07</span> </div> <div class="loader" id="loader">Loading model</div> </div> </section> Arrow SVGs: viewBox 0 0 24 24, fill none, stroke currentColor, stroke-width 2.6, round caps/joins. prev path: "M19 12H5M11 6l-6 6 6 6" next path: "M5 12h14M13 6l6 6-6 6" IMPORTANT: The big "Explore / New / Ideas" headline is NOT HTML text. It is drawn onto a 2D canvas inside WebGL so the glass cube can refract it (see section 4). The HTML only has a visually hidden <h1> for accessibility. ================================================== 3. CSS (exact values) ================================================== :root { --bg:#000; --fg:#fff; --pad-x: clamp(20px, 6.95vw, 120px) } html, body { height:100%; background:#000; color:#fff; font-family:'Poppins',sans-serif; -webkit-font-smoothing:antialiased } .hero { position:relative; width:100%; height:100vh; height:100svh; min-height:520px; overflow:hidden; background:#000 } #scene { position:absolute; inset:0; width:100%; height:100%; display:block; cursor:grab; touch-action:none } #scene.dragging { cursor:grabbing } .ui { position:absolute; inset:0; pointer-events:none; z-index:2 } /* drags pass through to the canvas */ .ui a, .ui button { pointer-events:auto } .sr-only { position:absolute; width:1px; height:1px; overflow:hidden; clip:rect(0 0 0 0); white-space:nowrap } NAV .nav { position:absolute; top:clamp(24px,4.7vh,40px); left:var(--pad-x); right:var(--pad-x); display:flex; align-items:center; justify-content:space-between } .logo { display:flex; align-items:center; gap:8px; color:#fff; text-decoration:none; font-size:15px; letter-spacing:-0.01em } .logo-mark { width:20px; height:40px; background:#fff; border-radius:0 20px 20px 0 } /* white "D" half-circle */ .logo b { font-weight:700 } .logo span { font-weight:400 } .nav-links { display:flex; gap:clamp(20px,4.1vw,60px); list-style:none } .nav-links a { color:#fff; text-decoration:none; font-size:15px; font-weight:500; position:relative } .nav-links a::after { content:''; position:absolute; left:0; right:0; bottom:-4px; height:1px; background:currentColor; transform:scaleX(0); transform-origin:right; transition:transform .35s ease } .nav-links a:hover::after { transform:scaleX(1); transform-origin:left } ARROWS (top-right, left of the dots column) .arrows { position:absolute; top:18.9%; left:76.7%; display:flex; gap:32px; transform:translate(-19px,-50%) } .arrow { width:38px; height:38px; border-radius:50%; border:2.5px solid #fff; background:transparent; color:#fff; display:grid; place-items:center; cursor:pointer; transition:background .25s, color .25s } .arrow svg { width:18px; height:18px } .arrow:hover { background:#fff; color:#000 } PAGINATION DOTS (vertical, right edge) .dots { position:absolute; right:calc(var(--pad-x) - 7px); top:49.4%; transform:translateY(-50%); display:flex; flex-direction:column; gap:33px } .dot { width:14px; height:14px; border-radius:50%; border:2px solid #fff; background:#fff; cursor:pointer; transition:background .25s } .dot.active { background:transparent } /* active = hollow ring, middle one active by default */ TAGLINE (bottom-left) .tagline { position:absolute; left:var(--pad-x); bottom:clamp(40px,7.5vh,70px); font-size:clamp(24px,2.65vw,44px); line-height:1.2; font-weight:300; letter-spacing:-0.01em } .tagline strong { font-weight:700; display:block } CTA ROW (button → horizontal line → giant outlined "07" bleeding off the right edge) .cta-row { position:absolute; left:45.6%; right:-1vw; top:88.7%; transform:translateY(-50%); display:flex; align-items:center } .cta { flex:none; padding:0 15px; height:48px; display:inline-flex; align-items:center; border:1.5px solid rgba(255,255,255,.85); border-radius:6px; background:rgba(0,0,0,.15); color:#fff; font-size:14px; font-weight:400; text-decoration:none; cursor:pointer; transition:background .25s, color .25s } .cta:hover { background:#fff; color:#000 } .cta-line { flex:1; height:1.5px; background:rgba(255,255,255,.8); min-width:40px } .count { flex:none; font-size:clamp(140px,19.8vw,360px); font-weight:400; line-height:1; letter-spacing:-0.02em; color:transparent; -webkit-text-stroke:1.5px rgba(255,255,255,.9); transform:translateY(6%); user-select:none } LOADER .loader { position:absolute; left:50%; top:50%; transform:translate(-50%,-50%); font-size:12px; letter-spacing:.2em; text-transform:uppercase; opacity:.6; transition:opacity .6s } .loader.done { opacity:0 } RESPONSIVE @media (max-width:900px), (max-aspect-ratio:1/1) { .arrows { left:auto; right:var(--pad-x); top:15%; transform:translateY(-50%); gap:14px } .tagline { bottom:clamp(150px,20vh,220px) } .cta-row { left:var(--pad-x); right:-3vw; top:auto; bottom:24px; transform:none } .count { font-size:clamp(120px,22vw,200px) } } @media (max-width:640px) { .nav-links { gap:16px } .nav-links a, .logo { font-size:13px } .dots { gap:20px; right:16px } .dot { width:10px; height:10px } .cta-row { right:-8vw } .count { font-size:120px } } @media (max-width:420px) { .nav-links li:nth-child(2) { display:none } } /* hide "Portfolio" */ No horizontal page scroll at any width. ================================================== 4. WEBGL SCENE (Three.js) ================================================== Renderer: WebGLRenderer({ canvas:#scene, antialias:true, alpha:false }), clearColor #000, outputColorSpace SRGBColorSpace, pixelRatio = min(devicePixelRatio, 2). Camera: PerspectiveCamera(fov 30, aspect W/H, 0.1, 100) at (0,0,10) looking at origin. 4a. Background headline (drawn into an offscreen 2D canvas → CanvasTexture) - Canvas size = viewport × DPR, filled #000. - mobile = (W < 768) || (W/H < 1). - fontSize fs = min(H*0.21, W*(mobile ? 0.21 : 0.118)); font = `800 ${fs}px Poppins`. If the widest line is wider than W*(mobile ? 0.9 : 0.5), scale fs down to fit. - Lines: "Explore", "New", "Ideas". Fill #e9e9e9, textAlign center, baseline alphabetic. - Centre x = W*(mobile ? 0.5 : 0.505); centre y = H*(mobile ? 0.45 : 0.468). Line gap = fs*1.07; cap height ≈ fs*0.7. Line i (0..2) baseline y = cy + cap/2 + (i-1)*gap. - Texture: colorSpace SRGB, LinearFilter, no mipmaps. Redraw on resize and on document.fonts 'loadingdone'. - Show it with a fullscreen quad (PlaneGeometry(2,2), ShaderMaterial, vertex outputs position.xy directly, fragment = texture2D(uTex, vUv) followed by #include <colorspace_fragment> ON ITS OWN LINE; depthTest/depthWrite false; frustumCulled false) in its own bgScene. - Wait for fonts before first draw: Promise.race([Promise.all([document.fonts.load('800 100px Poppins'), document.fonts.ready]), 2500ms timeout]) then layout() + start loop. 4b. Model loading - GLTFLoader.load(MODEL_URL). Traverse gltf.scene; for each mesh: clone geometry, delete 'uv','color','tangent' attributes, mergeVertices(g, 1e-4), computeVertexNormals(), applyMatrix4(mesh.matrixWorld). Merge all parts with mergeGeometries. - Centre the geometry on its bounding box and scale uniformly so its largest dimension = 1. - Scene graph: scene → pivot (screen position + scale) → spinner (rotation) → cube mesh. On load add class "done" to #loader. 4c. Cube placement (in layout(), on load and on resize) - visH = 2*tan(fov/2)*10; visW = visH*aspect. - Screen-fraction centre: sx = mobile ? 0.5 : 0.517, sy = mobile ? 0.45 : 0.488. pivot.position = ((sx-0.5)*visW, (0.5-sy)*visH, 0). - On-screen edge length px = min(H*0.44, W*(mobile ? 0.45 : 0.29)); pivot.scale = (px/H)*visH. - Initial spinner rotation: Euler(-0.42, 0.62, 0.18). 4d. Glass material — custom ShaderMaterial, screen-space refraction with 6-band chromatic dispersion, rendered in two passes (back faces, then front faces). Vertex shader: varying vec3 vNormal; varying vec3 vEye; worldPos = modelMatrix*position; mvPos = viewMatrix*worldPos; gl_Position = projectionMatrix*mvPos; vNormal = normalize(normalMatrix*normal); vEye = normalize(https://mvpos.xyz/); Fragment shader: uv = gl_FragCoord.xy / uResolution (drawing-buffer size). n = normalize(vNormal); if (uBackside > 0.5) n = -n; // do NOT use gl_FrontFacing, three.js flips winding for BackSide eye = normalize(vEye). LOOP = 16 iterations; slide = i/LOOP * 0.045. For each band compute refract(eye, n, 1.0/ior) with iorR/Y/G/C/B/P and sample uTexture at uv + refr.xy * (uRefractPower + slide*k) * uChromatic, with k = 1 (R), 1 (Y), 2 (G), 2.5 (C), 3 (B), 1 (P): r = tex(R).x*0.5 y = (tex(Y).x*2 + tex(Y).y*2 - tex(Y).z)/6 g = tex(G).y*0.5 c = (tex(C).y*2 + tex(C).z*2 - tex(C).x)/6 b = tex(B).z*0.5 p = (tex(P).z*2 + tex(P).x*2 - tex(P).y)/6 R = r + (2p + 2y - c)/3; G = g + (2y + 2c - p)/3; B = b + (2c + 2p - y)/3 color += vec3(R,G,B) color /= LOOP; saturation adjust: mix(luma(color), color, uSaturation) with luma weights (0.2125, 0.7154, 0.0721). Specular (Blinn-Phong, light vector = normalize(-light), view = -eye): spec = specular(uLight, uShininess, uDiffuseness) + 0.6 * specular(vec3(1,1,-1), uShininess*0.6, uDiffuseness*0.5) spec(x) = pow(max(dot(n,halfVec),0), shininess) + max(0,dot(n,lightVec))*diffuseness color += spec * (backside ? 0.35 : 1.0) Fresnel: f = pow(1.0 + dot(eye, n), uFresnelPower); color = mix(color, vec3(1), f * (backside ? 0.25 : 0.55)). color += vec3(0.004, 0.005, 0.007). gl_FragColor = vec4(color,1); then #include <colorspace_fragment> on its own line. Uniform values: uIorR 1.15, uIorY 1.16, uIorG 1.18, uIorC 1.22, uIorB 1.22, uIorP 1.22, uRefractPower 0.30 (front) / 0.22 (back), uChromatic 0.5, uSaturation 1.08, uShininess 90, uDiffuseness 0.02, uFresnelPower 5.0, uLight (-1, 1, 1), uBackside 0 (frontMat, side FrontSide) / 1 (backMat, side BackSide). 4e. Render pipeline (every frame) - Two WebGLRenderTargets sized to drawing buffer (W*DPR × H*DPR), type HalfFloatType, default (linear) colour space: rtBack, rtFront. - backMat.uTexture = rtBack.texture; frontMat.uTexture = rtFront.texture. 1) render bgScene → rtBack 2) render bgScene → rtFront, then (autoClear=false) cube with backMat → rtFront 3) render bgScene → screen, then (autoClear=false, clearDepth) cube with frontMat → screen - This gives the look: text seen through the cube is magnified, mirrored and split into blue/yellow fringes, inner rounded edges of the cube are faintly visible, and the bevelled edges glow white. ================================================== 5. INTERACTION & ANIMATION ================================================== - Drag to rotate (pointer events on the canvas, setPointerCapture): dx = Δx*0.008, dy = Δy*0.008; apply as world-space rotation: premultiply spinner.quaternion by axisAngle(Y, dx) then axisAngle(X, dy). Track velocity per 16.67ms frame; add class "dragging" to the canvas while dragging. - Inertia after release: keep applying velocity, damped by 0.94^(dt*60) per frame. - Idle drift: 0.6s after release, blend in a constant slow rotation of 0.0035 rad/frame around Y and 0.0012 rad/frame around X (blend ramps 0→1 over 1s). It also runs from page load. - Prev/Next arrow buttons: smoothly rotate the cube -90°/+90° around Y (ease: each frame apply remaining*min(1, 0.09*dt*60) until remaining < 0.0005). Cancels inertia; dragging cancels the spin. - Dots: clicking a dot makes it the only .active one (hollow ring). - Hover transitions: nav link underline wipe (.35s), arrow and CTA buttons invert to white bg / black content (.25s). - Clamp frame dt to 0.05s. Recompute layout (renderer size, camera aspect, render-target sizes, uResolution, headline canvas, cube position/scale) on window resize. ================================================== 6. LAYOUT REFERENCE (desktop 1440×806) ================================================== - Logo at (100, 38), 40px tall. Nav links right-aligned, right edge ≈ 1340, vertical centre ≈ 58. - Arrow circles centred at ≈ (1105, 152) and (1175, 152). - Dots at x ≈ 1340, y ≈ 351 / 398 / 445 (middle one hollow). - Headline "Explore / New / Ideas" centred at x ≈ 727, ~170px ExtraBold, baselines ≈ 272 / 445 / 637. - Glass cube occupies ≈ x 510–1000, y 145–600, slightly right of centre, overlapping the headline. - Tagline "Let's Build the / Future of / Design." at left 100, bottom ≈ 60px, ~38px, Light with Bold "Design.". - "Explore Now" button at (657, 691), 48px tall; a 1.5px line runs right to a huge outlined "07" whose "0" starts at x ≈ 1140 and whose "7" is clipped by the right and bottom edges. - Pure black background, all UI white. Mobile (≤767px or portrait): headline and cube centred at 50% x / 45% y, headline up to 90% width, arrows move under the nav on the right, tagline sits above the CTA row, and the CTA row is pinned 24px from the bottom with "07" partly off-screen on the right. Output: one complete index.html, nothing else.

summary.zh: 创作者用一份结构化长提示词让Opus 5.5以纯代码方式还原了参考视频的像素风动画效果，提示词涵盖输入素材、视觉风格、分镜结构和具体实现步骤，并用Playwright和ffmpeg渲染合成。
summary.en: A 20-second pixel-art style video recreating a referenced clip was built with Claude Opus 5.5 using a detailed structured prompt covering inputs, visual direction, scene-by-scene structure and build steps, rendered with Playwright and ffmpeg.

prompt.text:
<inputs>
Ask me for: a voiceover or song with a spoken line (the audio file) and its transcript, 10-12 small objects that sum up my life, two silhouettes to light like a heat camera (a head in profile and a raised hand), and the 3 words I want to land hardest. If I skip any, use the defaults: vinyl, book, camera, cat, coin, game controller, cap, heart, money, plant, clapperboard, skateboard; free CC0 silhouettes from Openverse; action, intention, curiosity.
</inputs>

<direction>
A 20 second 4:3 film, 1440x1080 at 60fps, cut to the voice. Off-white paper, black, one red, one yellow, Geist for every word. Film grain on everything, a soft vignette, and a camera that never rests: a slow handheld float under everything plus a slow push inside every scene.
No scene cuts to the next: each handoff starts on the exact last frame of the scene before. The only hard cuts are the beat flips on the last word.
Every object is pixel art you draw yourself: a 16x16 grid per object, every cell a hand-placed colour, rendered as a 3D block (a darker extrusion down-right, a thin bevel on every cell) with a soft contact shadow.
The silhouettes are lit like a heat camera: the heat comes from how thick the body is at each point, so the nose, the hair and the fingertips run cooler, plus one hotspot and a slow moving noise, mapped through a black > red > orange > cream ramp. The edge stays razor sharp, with a soft glow outside it.
Motion rules: nothing pops in (eased glides of about 0.5s with a soft start), fast moves get real motion blur instead of ghost copies, and captions type with the voice behind a block cursor.
Banned: stock footage, AI video, 3D camera moves, particles, glitch.
</direction>

<structure>
Hang every scene on the transcript's word timings (measure them with faster-whisper word timestamps, one short chunk at a time):
1. The first word fills a yellow card. The card wipes off to the left and the question types underneath on two centred lines that glide to stay centred as they grow, the key word underlined in red as it's spoken.
2. The objects streak past in lanes above and below the words, a cyan four-point flare sweeps in, then the page burns away: black closes in from the edges onto the head, behind a hot red edge.
3. The head heats up on black while the answer types low on the left. A thin white orbit draws itself around the head, its far half passing behind it. On the last word, paper blooms out from inside the head with the objects in it, and the camera falls through: the head rushes past the lens until the paper is all we see.
4. The objects sit on a tilted ring seen in perspective (the front ones bigger and lower, drawn last), slowly turning, each one bobbing; the coin flips and lands with sparks.
5. On each of the 3 words, that object flies out of the ring to the left and grows, the page floods black from it, and the word types beside it (camera: a red shutter star; book: a red ribbon sweep; record: two white orbits and red notes). Then the flood drains back into the object as it flies home, and the camera dives closer into the ring. Put each hero object in the slot that is front-left when its word lands.
6. The ring pulls in a touch, bursts outward, every object turns to ink, and ink blots grow and swallow the page.
7. The hand rises into frame, hot, with the line split either side of it. The heart drops into its palm, then lifts to the centre at the size the next scene holds it.
8. The last word, one letter per beat, the background flipping paper / black / red, the heart holding its place across the cut, the centre object morphing pixel by pixel into the next one.
9. Thin brush strokes sweep through, the letters drift apart and float, then settle back into the word with the heart above it. The camera keeps pushing through the hold.
</structure>

<build>
1. One HTML canvas. Every frame is a pure function of time inside seek(t).
2. Bake each pixel sprite once to an offscreen canvas (the extrusion layers, then the face), then draw it scaled and rotated.
3. The heat: precompute each silhouette's base heat once (a distance transform of the mask, held at the edge value outside it so nothing dark bleeds in when it is upscaled). Every frame, add the hotspot and two octaves of value noise at quarter resolution, map it through a 256-step lookup, upscale it, and cut it with the full-resolution mask.
4. The fall through the head: draw the ring scene into an offscreen layer, mask it with the head scaled up about a point inside the skull, and grow that scale on a cubed curve until the head covers the frame. The ring inside zooms less than the head does, so it reads as depth.
5. The pixel morph: pair every cell of object A with a cell of object B and glide each one's position and colour, with a small random delay per cell.
6. Render with Playwright at 60fps with 8 motion-blur subframes, then lay the original audio back on with ffmpeg.
</build>

<gotchas>
A mask PNG with no alpha channel fills the whole box with heat, so put the silhouette in the alpha. A limb cut by the photo's border shows as a straight edge, so extend the mask past the frame. A handoff only reads as smooth when the last frame of one scene is the first frame of the next: draw the outgoing scene under the transition, and give scenes that show the same ring one shared zoom function. A flood that's still retreating when the next scene starts reads as a hard cut, so let it finish first. A fast ease-out flood reads as a jump; use a soft start.
</gotchas>

<start>
Ask me for the inputs, measure the word timings, then show me 8 stills before you render.
</start>

summary.en: A vertical 2D cartoon animal-facts Short with a narrating host, built in code with Claude Opus 5.5. The posted prompt covers script, image sheets, cutouts, lip-sync, ElevenLabs voice, canvas rendering and mixing.

prompt.text:
<inputs>
Ask me for my animal or topic ("Why is the X the most disturbing animal in the ocean?", "Why is X terrifying?"), or pitch 3, each with 5 true facts that get worse as they go. Ask which image model I have (GPT Image 2 or any model that takes a reference image at 4K, about $0.03 an image) and which voice I have (ElevenLabs, or Kokoro for free). Then write the script and the shot list with seconds, and show me both before anything costs money.
</inputs>

<direction>
A 1080x1920, 60 fps, 30-35 s vertical Short in the style of the big narrated animal-facts channels where a guy in a hoodie with a mic pops into every scene. Here everything is a flat 2D cartoon: thick dark brown outlines (#1f1418), flat colours, simple cel shading, big round googly eyes.
The host: a cartoon young man with messy brown hair, glasses, a plain heather grey hoodie with no logo, dark jeans, white sneakers, always holding a black mic.
- He is about 1000-1050 px tall on screen. His feet sit below the frame edge, so he is cut off at the shins.
- He pops up from below the frame in 0.32 s with an overshoot ease.
- His mouth flaps on the voice whenever he talks to camera.
- His face always stays above the caption pill.
The animal: one character in 9 poses (neutral, shocked, angry, plus costume poses for the facts: old with a beard and cane, a powdered wig, a teen with braces, drunk, a front view of the face, defeated on a plate). One costume per fact is the joke.
A new place every 1.5-3 s. Never repeat a composition.
Something always moves:
- Animals swim with a tail wave and bob ±10 px.
- The camera pushes in 2-4% per shot.
- Pose swaps squash.
- Hits shake the frame.
Titles are one or two big words per beat in Luckiest Guy (Google Fonts), 104-190 px at y 430, tilted ±0.03-0.05 rad:
- They wobble ±0.025 rad.
- The outline is 0.22 of the size in #1f1418, with a darker copy of the colour 0.09 of the size underneath.
- Colours are pairs of fill and shadow: yellow #ffd21f/#c27a10, red #ff4a3d/#8e1a14, white #ffffff/#9aa6b4, pink #ff7ab8/#a8336d, green #7dff6a/#2e9a2a.
Captions:
- 1-4 words in a white pill at y 1470: Luckiest Guy 66 px, dark text, a 7 px outline, pill height 1.55x the text.
- The key word is yellow with a dark outline.
- The pill pops from 0.82 to 1 in 0.13 s.
A red marker ellipse circles the animal when its name is said.
Banned: photoreal cutouts mixed into cartoon art, a real person's face, the real channel's logo or name on screen, a still frame over 1 s, the host covering the animal's face on its key word.
</direction>

<structure>
Length: 30-35 s, about 115 words at about 3.5 words a second. Times are from a 33.5 s film; scale them to the voice.
0-1.9 s, the hook "Why is the X the most disturbing animal in the ocean?":
- The animal glides in from off screen in 0.75 s while the host pops up bottom right, already talking.
- On the animal's name: a red ring, the name as a title, and the host swaps to pointing at it for 0.7 s.
1.9-3.7 s: a punch-in on "disturbing". The water is graded red, the angry pose, an impact starburst, the word in red.
3.7-8.2 s, fact 1, the shocking number:
- A counter rolls up to it.
- Then a comparison everyone gets ("older than America") shown as a costume pose and a prop that springs in.
8.2-12.7 s, facts 2 and 3 played as gags:
- One is a costume in a new place.
- One is a race the animal loses. On "slower than you walk", the host strolls past it.
12.7-15.6 s: the gross detail, with a zoom into the face.
15.6-16.7 s: "But it gets worse." A red alarm grade with a pulsing vignette. The animal yells into the lens and the host swaps from talking to horrified.
16.7-21 s, the worst fact:
- The host cowers behind the victim, which then vanishes in a poof.
- An x-ray shot shows what is inside.
21-27.7 s: the human angle, each line with a person from the cast acting it out. The host joins in (drunk next to the drunk Viking).
27.7-29 s: someone happily eats it while the host turns green and gags.
29-33.5 s: the callback joke that ties back to the hook. The host talks to camera, then cracks up on the last word. Hold 1.15 s after the last word.
</structure>

<build>
1. Tools: Python, Playwright with Chromium or Edge, FFmpeg, OpenCV, Pillow, numpy, soundfile. Install what's missing and tell me what you installed.
2. Art, 4 images in total (about $0.12). Every prompt starts with "Match the exact art style of the reference image: flat 2D cartoon, thick dark brown outlines, flat colours with simple cel shading, big expressive googly eyes, clean vector look". Feed the first sheet you like back in as the style reference for the rest.
- Animal sheet: 1:1 at 4K, "a 3 by 3 pose sheet of the SAME cartoon X, 9 separate poses on plain pure white, plenty of white space, nothing touching, no grid lines, no text, no ground shadows", every pose a full side view facing right except the front face.
- Cast sheet: 1:1 at 4K, 9 different characters and props for the facts, same wording.
- Background grid: 9:16 at 4K, "a 3 by 3 grid of 9 equal tall vertical panels separated by thin white gutters, each panel an EMPTY scene, no characters, no text, keep the lower middle open".
- Host sheet: 9:16 at 4K, 9 full-body poses at the same size: (1) facing the viewer, mic below the chin, mouth CLOSED, (2) EXACTLY the same pose with only the mouth WIDE OPEN, (3) talking and pointing to the side, (4) horrified with a hand on the cheek, (5) crouching and cowering with sweat drops, (6) running in side view facing right, (7) laughing and leaning back, (8) gagging with a green face holding a toothpick of food, (9) drunk with spiral eyes.
3. Cutouts:
- Flood the white from the border (seeds every 64 px around the edge) with a floating range of 7, so soft glows go too.
- Feather a 3 px band outside the shapes with alpha = clamp((250 - min(R,G,B)) / 150). Un-mix the white from that band: colour = (c - 255(1 - a)) / a.
- Group the pieces by the grid cell their centre falls in and drop pieces under 150 px.
- Split the background grid on its white gutters (rows and columns whose minimum channel averages over 232). Crop 4 px in, cover-fit to 1080x1920 with Lanczos, unsharp mask (radius 2, 60%).
4. Host lip-sync:
- Align pose 2 onto pose 1 by template-matching the glasses and eyes. Paste only its mouth onto pose 1 through a feathered ellipse (sigma 4). Now open and closed are the same drawing, so the outline never wobbles.
- Mouth track at 60 fps from the voice: RMS per frame, smoothed over 3 frames. Open when it is over (70th percentile in dB - 15) and over 0.55x the loudest frame within ±0.1 s.
- Hold every state at least 3 frames. Break open runs longer than 14 frames with a 3-frame close every 12 frames. That gives about 8 flips a second.
- Anchor every host pose by its feet and its head centre x (the alpha centre of the top 28% of the cutout), so pose swaps never jump. Measure that per pose.
5. Voice: ElevenLabs eleven_v4 with the timestamps endpoint, a calm deep documentary narrator, stability 0.5, similarity 0.75, one take (about 300 credits for 600 characters).
- Cut pauses (10 ms frames under -40 dB, longer than 0.2 s) down to their first and last 0.06 s, with 8 ms fades.
- Then atempo 1.15 and a 0.15 s lead-in.
- Rebuild word times from the character alignment through the same cuts and tempo. When a start lands after the next word's start, pull it back.
- Free route: Kokoro, then whisper for the word times.
6. Film: one HTML canvas where every frame is a pure function of time: window .seek(t), READY, END, and EV with the sound times. One function per shot.
- Sprite tail wave: draw the cutout in 28 vertical slices. Each slice moves dy = sin(8t - 4.5u) * wig * k, where k = (max(0, u - 0.3) / 0.7)^1.5 and wig is 3-14 px.
- Pop: 1 - 0.6 e^(-9Δt) cos(20Δt). Pose-swap kick: 1 + a e^(-10Δt) cos(22Δt), with a = 0.1-0.22. Shake: A e^(-7Δt) sin(61Δt), with A = 22-34 px.
- Props drawn in code: a rolling number counter, a waving flag, a flipping calendar, green fumes, buzzing flies, confetti, red rings, arrows, an impact starburst, poof clouds, bubbles.
- Red alarm grade: grayscale(.5) sepia(1) hue-rotate(-35deg) saturate(3.2) brightness(.55).
- X-ray: grayscale(1) invert(1) sepia(1) hue-rotate(150deg) saturate(3.5) on #071a2e with a 60 px cyan grid and a scan line.
- Look up repeated words by their occurrence (the third "and"), or cuts land on the wrong line.
7. Check, render, sound:
- Contact sheets of 12-15 frames at key words before rendering. Fix covered faces, the host over the animal's face, and titles off screen.
- Render 60 fps with 8 motion-blur subframes over half a frame, then libx264 CRF 19.
- Music: a quirky piano mystery bed, free on Pixabay, with the voice 11-14 dB over it in every phrase.
- Mixkit SFX, one per event, placed by their peaks: a pop on every title, a whoosh when the host or the animal enters, a hit on the big beats, a bite, a boing, a sad trombone on the fails, a poof, bubbles.
- Mix to -14 LUFS.
</build>

<gotchas>
- A plain hue tint for the red alarm turned blue water green. Sepia first, then hue-rotate.
- Long titles overflow at 160 px. Split them into two beats ("OLDER THAN", then "AMERICA" in red).
- The host walking past on the key word hid the animal's face. Time his pass after the key word, keep him lower and smaller (0.62 scale), or draw him behind.
- Photoreal sticker animals with code eyes read as slop next to a real presenter. One flat cartoon style for everything fixes it.
- If the two talking poses differ by more than the mouth, swapping whole images makes the outline wobble. Paste the mouth only.
</gotchas>

<start>
Ask me for my animal or topic, or pitch 3, then show me the script and the shot list.
</start>

summary.en: The prompt asked for a self-contained Three.js browser experience featuring a soft-body jelly pufferfish with inflation, interaction, animation, materials, controls and sound.

prompt.text:
Build an interactive 3D jelly pufferfish (fugu) as a single self-contained HTML page using three.js from a CDN.

The fish is a soft-body gummy sitting on a table. Model the body as one closed icosphere-topology skin with two rest shapes per vertex: a calm fish (blunt round head, body tapering to a short tail stalk, slightly flattened belly) and a fully inflated ball (sphere with the same tail stalk sticking out). Blend between them with an "inflation" value. Simulate with XPBD at a fixed 1/600 s substep (frame-rate independent): edge-length constraints, a global volume constraint, a soft global shape-matching pull toward the blended rest shape (rotation via polar decomposition, gently leaning upright), ground collision with friction, and damping applied to the wobble (velocity relative to the body's mean) so it jiggles but settles in about a second. Render with one Loop-subdivision pass for a smooth surface.

Behaviour: tapping the fish startles it. It gulps air three times (mouth opens on each gulp, small overshoot) until it is a round ball, stays puffed about 4 seconds, then slowly deflates while blowing iridescent bubbles from its mouth. Dragging grabs and stretches the jelly locally; dragging empty space orbits the camera; wheel or pinch zooms.

Details: ~260 soft spines that lie flat and hidden when calm, pop up one by one (staggered) as it inflates, wobble on their own springs, bend against the table, and lift the ball so it stands on its spines. Big glossy eyes (gold-green iris, large pupil, white catchlight) that follow the cursor. Puckered lips with a tiny white beak. Translucent ray-striped fins: fluttering pectorals, swaying tail fan, rippling dorsal and anal fins, all faster when alarmed. Dark freckles on the back, pale belly, a few air bubbles trapped inside the jelly.

Look: MeshPhysicalMaterial with transmission, clearcoat and sheen for a candy-gummy look; a soft environment map; a soft colored shadow with a faint caustic on a floor that matches the page background. Flavour presets Yuzu, Ramune, Momo, Matcha. Editorial "Material Studies" layout: big italic serif title "Fugu Jelly.", a side panel with flavour swatches, Firmness and Wobble sliders, Startle / Calm / Reset buttons, ¼ speed and Sound toggles, and live readouts for volume, spine angle and mood. Synthesized WebAudio sounds for gulps, a boing on tap, a hiss while deflating and tiny bubble pops. Responsive down to phone width.

prompt.text:
架空の大型ロケット（2段式の液体ロケット＋固体ブースター2本、白い機体、名前なし）と
その射点について、CAD図面と Blender 動画を作ってください。

【図面】2D の DXF のみ（3Dモデルの書き出しは不要）。単位 mm、A2 の図枠と表題欄つき。
線は青緑系の「電子の図面」風にし、プレビュー画像は濃紺の背景にする。
1. 射点配置図 S=1:500（ロケットを原点に置き、実際の位置で描く。
移動発射台・排煙溝・アンビリカルタワー・避雷塔・照明塔・水タンク・建屋・海岸線）
2. 射点立面図（南から）S=1:400
3. ロケット外形図・断面図 S=1:250
特記事項に「架空の機体・射場のイメージで、実在の図面ではない」と書く。
寸法は Python の形状モジュール1つで決め、図面と動画の両方がそれを読み込む。

【動画】Blender（EEVEE）、1920×1080・24fps・本編20秒＋ロゴ3.5秒、音つき MP4。
1. 暗闇の床に、シアンに光る射点配置図が中心から走査されて描かれる（真上から）
2. 図面の線が光のワイヤーとして立ち上がる
3. 光の粒（Geometry Nodes）が渦を巻いて昇り、発射台・タワー・ロケットが下から積み上がる
（積み上がった高さより下だけが実体になる。カメラは寄る）
4. 図面がマス目ごとにデジタルに溶け、夜の射点が現れる（海・丘・星空。カメラは引く）。
照明塔が点いて白い機体が浮かび、塔の頂部の赤い灯が明滅する
5. アクセスアームが離れる → カウントダウン → 点火 → リフトオフ。
炎は発光する円錐、噴煙は排煙溝と発射台から湧き、上昇する機体の後ろに煙の柱が残る
6. 上昇するロケットを海の上から見上げたところでタイトル → 最後に指定のロゴ
音は外部素材を使わず Python で合成する
（電子音の BGM、波、カウントダウンの電子音、点火から上昇までの轟音、タイトルの和音）。

【進め方】
- 図面のプレビュー画像を目で見て、文字の重なりを直す
- 本番の前にテスト静止画を数枚描いて確認する（照明の明るさ、炎や光の白飛び）
- 本番レンダーは軽い設定で、PC を休ませながら回す。始める前に所要時間を伝えて了承を取る

summary.en: A Satoru Gojo anime music video edit made with Claude Opus 5.5 from Midjourney images and a music file, with no video footage. The creator shared the full prompt in a reply.

prompt.text:
Create a spectacular 4:3 Jujutsu Kaisen AMV centered on Satoru Gojo, using the supplied images and music. Match the final video's duration exactly to the full soundtrack.

EDITING & ANIMATION:
Analyze the music's rhythm, structure, energy and emotional progression. Animate the supplied images into dynamic cinematic sequences with expressive character motion, dramatic camera movements, parallax and seamless transitions. Creatively select, crop, reframe, combine and revisit images throughout the edit. Build an intense anime opening with powerful visual storytelling, synchronized precisely to the music.

DYNAMIC GRID:
Use a constantly evolving manga-inspired grid with variable cell sizes, shapes and arrangements. Mix large hero panels, small square cells, narrow strips, irregular rectangles and occasional diagonal divisions. Freely expand, shrink, split, merge and rearrange cells according to the music. Alternate between dense multi-cell compositions, striking asymmetrical layouts and occasional full-frame hero moments. Allow different images, perspectives and moments to coexist across cells. Keep panel boundaries crisp and compositions visually coherent.

VISUAL EFFECTS:
Create intense, layered effects inspired by Gojo Satoru's powers and the visual identity of Jujutsu Kaisen. Explore spatial distortion, Infinity, Six Eyes, cursed energy, Blue, Red and Hollow Purple through inventive motion graphics, impact frames, dimensional fractures and cinematic transitions. Blend style infections spreading across neighboring cells with temporal echoes, frame repetitions, speed ramps, freezes and rhythmic chain reactions. Let effects interact creatively with the grid and occasionally break beyond panel boundaries.

CREATIVE DIRECTION:
Make this feel like a premium, visually groundbreaking Jujutsu Kaisen anime opening. Capture Gojo's overwhelming power, confidence, elegance and mysterious presence. Let the supplied images and soundtrack guide every creative decision, including pacing, visual treatments, transitions, color grading and effect intensity. Avoid repetitive editing patterns or generic templates. Balance explosive action with striking moments of visual clarity. Preserve Gojo's recognizable identity, facial features, costume and the artistic style of the supplied images.

AUDIO:
Use the supplied music as the primary soundtrack, uninterrupted from beginning to end. Synchronize animation, grid transformations, camera movements and visual effects to its beats, melodies, transitions and emotional peaks.
No typography, text, letters, numbers or watermarks.

prompt.text:
Make a 45-second paper-collage animation of Momotaro (the Japanese folktale).

[Look]
A pop-up picture book: the book opens and paper pieces stand up one by one.
Washi paper cut-out (kirie) texture. The 3D effect comes from images and code only. Do not use any video-generation AI.

[How to build it]
1. First, write the script and show it to me (8 scenes, 4-9 seconds each; the only on-screen text is short onomatopoeia such as "donburako").
2. Once I approve the script, write the image-generation prompts:
- one texture reference image
- characters and backgrounds as sheets of separate paper cut-outs on transparent backgrounds
3. I will generate the images and hand them to you. Then animate them in Python:
- make it look 3D with five tricks: depth, parallax, blur, shadows, and motion blur
- 1920x1080, 24 fps
- for each scene, show me 4 still frames first so I can check
4. Add narration and background music.

[Rules]
- Do not wobble or shake the pictures. Movement is only slow pushes in and pulls back.
- Don't give me English-only prompts; add an explanation in my language too.

prompt.text:
Create a single self-contained HTML file using Three.js that renders a beautiful animated voxel-art 3D scene. A giant woolly mammoth walks across a sea of clouds through a snowy night with the northern lights and a moon; the clouds drift backwards under its feet, and snow puffs up at every step.

On its back, over a blue blanket with gold trim and leather straps, stands a stone frost fortress: walls with battlements, four round turrets with blue conical roofs and flags, two small houses with glowing windows and smoking chimneys, and a central keep with a big glowing ice crystal floating and slowly rotating above it. The mammoth has shaggy fur, a swaying trunk, long curved tusks and snow on its head.

A crystalline ice dragon with horns, ice spikes along its back, glowing eyes and large wings rises from the clouds and circles the mammoth, leaving a trail of snowflakes, and breathes frost twice.

Add soft shadows, voxel ambient occlusion, a snowstorm, drifting voxel clouds and a slow cinematic camera orbit. Make it as detailed and polished as possible.

prompt.text:
Make "Plush Watermelon" (Material Studies No. 032) on the Plush Penguin WebGPU engine: XPBD soft-body lattice, shell fur, cloth limbs, posture-driven gait, Hand / Finger / Comb tools.

Shape (one SDF):
- A fat wedge cut from a sphere by two planes through one horizontal axis, about 76° apart.
- The axis is the top edge, so each cut face is a semicircle.
- The cut faces are slightly puffy and every seam is rounded.
- It sits on a small flat patch of its round rind.

Regions:
- Flesh: long fluffy red minky.
- Rind: a white band along the outer edge of both faces.
- Skin: green, with dark jagged stripes running pole to pole around the wedge's axis.
- Seeds: short-pile felt teardrops pointing in toward the axis, a few on the front face around the face, more on the back.

Front face: two bead eyes, rosy cheeks, and an embroidered smile thread laid into a short-pile groove.

Limbs: two brown felt legs stuck out in front, and two stubby felt cloth arms at the wedge's ends.

Actions:
- Toddle: walk on the legs.
- Rock: seesaw forward and back on the rind with a synthesized giggle.
- Wave: arm waves and hops with a toy squeak.
- Topple: fall onto its back, then get back up.
- A finger boop on the face makes it giggle and rock; it also rocks now and then when idle.

Palettes: Classic, Yellow, Sorbet.
Readouts: mass, volume, steps, rocks.

summary.zh: 这是一个单文件 HTML 三维机械巨型鱿鱼模拟器，包含程序化建模、拆解动画、交互控制、遥测界面、视频采集和合成音频。Opus 5.5 根据单条提示生成了它。
summary.en: A self-contained HTML file presents a procedural 3D robotic giant squid with animated teardown scenes, controls, telemetry, capture support, and synthesized audio. Opus 5.5 generated it from one prompt.

prompt.text:
Build a single self-contained HTML file: an interactive, fully procedural 3D robotic giant squid called "Architeuthis AX-10" (brand mark "Teuthis"), rendered with three.js r170 loaded via an importmap from jsDelivr. No external models, textures or images; every part is generated in code at load time. Target quality: a premium product-simulator / engineering teardown page with thousands of real moving parts.

LOOK
- Bright studio look: near-white background (canvas-drawn, soft lavender corner gradients, faint dot grid top-right), white glossy shells with clearcoat, near-black mechanical internals, violet accents (#8a4dff) and glowing violet emissives.
- No tone mapping; calibrate lights so white shells stay just below 1.0 and keep visible shading (no blown-out whites). Hemisphere + key directional light with soft PCF shadows (2048 map) + fill + rim + RoomEnvironment PMREM reflections. Invisible shadow-catcher floor plus a soft contact shadow blob.
- Post: EffectComposer with HalfFloat MSAA target, GTAO (hide background, floor, emissives and decorative lines during the AO prepass), UnrealBloom with a high threshold (~1.5) so only emissive parts glow, OutputPass.
- Procedural surface-detail shader injected into MeshPhysicalMaterial via onBeforeCompile: clustered drill holes, short slots, rivet rows parallel to every panel edge, and a dark seam groove along panel borders. Geometry builders write per-vertex metric surface coordinates and distance-to-panel-edge attributes so holes stay round and evenly sized; antialias with fwidth; holes kill clearcoat; per-instance seed so instanced links differ.

GEOMETRY TOOLKIT
- revPanel(): surface-of-revolution panel with real thickness (outer, inner, flat-shaded rims), profile from Catmull-Rom-smoothed points, angular range, offset. Plus extruded gears, spline tubes/cables, rounded boxes. Merge each part's geometry per material.

MODEL (body frame: +z toward the arms, +y dorsal)
- Mantle (~1.2 m ogive cone) on a neck joint so it can swing relative to the head: 28 separate shell panels with gaps, hinge knuckles, violet tiles, LEDs and vent slots; a hinged glass window along the top that opens 110° (hinge axis computed from the panel edge); under it 8 lit violet piston bays, each with 16–24 black components, pistons with steel rods, capacitors, coils, headers; dark inner hull; tail cap with glowing tip; collar ring with 60 bolts.
- Head (slightly enlarged sub-frame): 15 shell strips, each auto-populated without overlaps with printed glyphs (Y, arrows, T, X), inset hatches with four screws, vent grilles, sensor ports with LEDs, steel grab rails, seam hinges; two antennas at the back.
- Visor plate on 6 steel lift pins. Under it a deep head cavity lined with a glowing violet motherboard: finned heat-sink processor, 7-blade spinning cooling fan, 3-ring gimballed gyro (rings spin on different axes), capacitor bank, twin steel coolant lines, cable harnesses to the eyes, ribbon cable, 3-gear head drive with correct ratios, and a sensor deck with a sonar puck on standoffs that lifts away.
- Two eyes: white donut housings with bolts, black glossy lens, glowing violet rings and glyph, 4 threaded telescoping barrel rings, 10-blade iris (each blade pivots), sapphire glass dome with rim.
- Dark hub under the head with ring gear, motors and cables; a central siphon with 3 nested telescoping sleeves and a 10-blade turbine whose glow follows thrust.

ARMS
- 8 arms (20 links) + 2 longer tentacles (30 links, clubbed). Links are built in unit-radius space with length = 2 × radius so everything scales uniformly; radius tapers from ~6 cm.
- Per link, GPU-instanced pieces: white or violet shell (two variants), ball joint with steel pin, chain side plates, two violet roller wheels with dark hubs on the oral side, plus occasional side modules, dorsal tiles and violet bands. Update all instance matrices on the CPU every frame.
- Quaternion forward kinematics: root frame spreads around a crown axis blended between the body axis and world-down (so arms splay octopus-like on the floor); per-link curvature = base bend + log-spiral tip term (curvature ∝ 1/remaining length, rollers inside the curl) + travelling wave; per-arm random variation. Blend poses: standing, jetting bundle, single arm stretched. Auto-ground the body so the lowest link touches the floor.

RIG AND TIMELINE
- Every rigid part is a registered group with base transform, chapter offsets and an explode vector; explode cascades with per-part delays, ease5 and free spin. Spin phases use the integral of a trapezoid speed profile so everything is deterministic.
- A pure stateAt(t) function (no accumulation) drives a ~28 s loop: jetting in mantle-first, settle and stand, Optics (barrels extend, iris cycles, dome lifts), Head core (visor lifts, then deck lifts while the camera slowly orbits the open cavity), Arm (one arm straightens, shells lift off the roller chain, spiral tip), Mantle (glass window opens over lit bays), Siphon (sleeves telescope, turbine spins up), Teardown (all parts free with a 360° turntable), Reassembly, Launch (arms bundle, jet off).
- Per-chapter camera shots computed in body axes with eased blends; decorative thin orbit lines with node markers around the camera target.

UI (HTML/CSS/SVG overlay, Inter Tight + IBM Plex Mono)
- Logo top-left, "Live sim" pill top-right, centered model line + title "Colossal Squid, Lens to Siphon" + date, chapter pills, left nav with sub-lines, right telemetry cards (mantle pressure kPa with 6 s sparkline computed from stateAt, jet thrust bar, arm load bars for 10 arms from real curvature, battery), bottom status "Chapter · NN% apart" with progress track and timecode.
- 3D-anchored callouts: anchor dot on the real part, leader line, white label card; two columns with collision spacing.
- Clicking a pill/nav item seeks the timeline with a smooth camera blend; drag to orbit (free camera); double-click or R returns to auto camera; space pauses; click the track to seek. Responsive phone layout, prefers-reduced-motion support, adaptive quality governor (fewer GTAO samples, then DPR 1, then GTAO off).

CAPTURE AND AUDIO
- Expose https://window.sim.seek/(t) for deterministic frame capture (capture mode: no rAF loop, CSS transitions off). Render 1920×1080 at 60 fps with headless Playwright, sampling the timeline at 1.68× so the video is exactly 17 s; encode H.264 CRF 17 with AAC audio.
- Original synthesized score (numpy/scipy, no samples), one bar = one chapter so every change lands on a downbeat, plus synced sound design: jet roar, servos, lens clicks, visor hiss, fan spin-up, gear ticks, gyro tinks, chain clatter, glass ting, piston thumps, turbine spin-up, teardown impact with hundreds of part clinks, reverse swell into reassembly, launch roar. Normalize to about −21 LUFS.

create a music video for this entire song, check lyrics.txt to sync the visuals to. style should be a mix between monty-python/vox style "postcards in space" mixed with sketchy ballpoint pen style visuals. this needs to look professional. theme of the video is a creepy evil pizza parlor, camera starts outside and works through the inside, through a secret bookshelf door into a basement with untold horrors and pizza sauce all over the place. use whatever tools or methods you need to make this look professional. final export should be an .mp4 of the entire music video.

prompt.text:
Apply a dark neon glitch-art effect to the attached video (Python + ffmpeg, frame by frame):

1. Cut out the subject with rembg (isnet-anime for anime/illustration, isnet-general-use for real footage). Make the background pure black.
2. Posterize the subject to 5 brightness levels and recolor it with a 3-color palette on black:
main color for cool/neutral areas (cyan #14b8f0), mid color (violet #6438c4), accent for warm/red areas (magenta #ff2ad4).
Keep it dark: most of the image black or navy, only the highlights glow. Let the color-patch edges crawl slightly with noise.
3. Add a magenta rim light on the subject's left edge.
4. Datamosh: wherever the current frame is empty, keep the previous frame shifted a few px down and faded (melting ghost trails). Also copy ~3% of 24px blocks from the previous frame with a small random offset.
5. Vertical drips: in ~30% of the columns, smear bright pixels upward (up to ~300px) and downward (~150px). Mix 2–8px wide drips with thin vertical scratch lines in the palette colors, denser near the subject.
6. Light grain + vignette. Keep the original resolution and fps, export as H.264 MP4.

Generate an original vaporwave-glitch soundtrack (~-12 LUFS) / make it a seamless loop where the last 1s drips into the first 1s column by column.

Build a cinematic 3D animation of a white Tesla Roadster performing a rocket-assisted stunt inside a massive nighttime test facility.

Start with a wide shot revealing a towering curved ramp supported by exposed steel scaffolding. Add red illuminated track edges, road markings, and industrial floodlights.

Follow the Roadster as it accelerates up the ramp, climbs vertically, and launches into open air.

At the highest point, switch to a dramatic low-angle close-up. Fire the downward-facing thrusters. Show bright exhaust and thick, rolling smoke that expands naturally beneath the car.

Bring it down onto the track, let the suspension compress on landing, then pull the camera back as it drives forward through the clearing smoke.

Keep the white bodywork readable throughout. Control headlight bloom. Make the wheels rotate correctly and keep the vehicle’s shape consistent between shots.

Add subtle circular HUD gauges for altitude and G-force.

16 seconds. Vertical 9:16 framing. Smooth camera movement.

Make it look expensive. The launch and thruster
